s1.quote: 50cm visibility is considered good by the diving team … The London is regularly dived by the volunteer licenced team led by diver Steve Ellis

s2.quote: Protection of Wrecks Act (1973) … Although the underwater dive conditions are difficult with limited visibility

access.value: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); diving only under licence, by the licensee's volunteer team

hazards.text: Very poor visibility, around 50 cm on a good day

summary.text: The 1665 warship London lies in two pieces in the Thames Estuary off Southend. It is a legally protected wreck worked by a licensed volunteer dive team in very murky water, so it is not a casual recreational dive.

sites.name: HMT Amethyst

s1.publisher: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record
s1.quote: least echosounder depth 15.8 in general depth 18.7m. Scour depth 22.4m … Large wreck and easy to locate

s2.quote: struck a mine in Barrow Deep in the Thames Estuary and sank

summary.text: An anti-submarine trawler sunk by a mine in 1940 in the Barrow Deep, Thames Estuary. Survey records show a sizeable, easily found wreck with a scour hole, its shallowest part around 16 m below chart datum.

sites.depthNote: Least depth 15.8 m, general seabed 18.7 m (LAT soundings); scour to 22.4 m

sites.name: HMS Venetia

s1.publisher: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record
s1.quote: Least depth by echo sounder 43.7ft in general depth 48ft. Scour 52ft … Dispersed and difficult to find

s2.quote: struck a mine off Knob Buoy in the Thames Estuary

hazards.text: Wreck dispersed and hard to find

summary.text: A First World War-era destroyer mined in the Thames Estuary in December 1940. Hydrographic surveys describe broken-up wreckage in roughly 14-15 m, with a scour beside it, and it has been hard to locate.

sites.depthNote: Least depth 43.7 ft, general 48 ft, scour 52 ft (1973 survey, LAT)

s1.publisher: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record
s1.quote: There has been no archaeological investigation of the site since designation as the sand has reburied the site

notDiveSite.reason: Protected wreck reburied under at least six metres of sand; not diveable

sites.name: HMS Whirlwind

s1.publisher: Coflein (Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales)
s1.quote: The wreck of HMS WHIRLWIND lies in 31m of water … It is reported as being collapsed and lying on its port side

s2.quote: it is also at a comfortably accessible depth of 36m … Slack water is essential … could put you well into decompression

hazards.text: Easy to run into decompression on one dive

highlights.text: Cold War frigate with a relatively intact hull

summary.text: A Cold War frigate that foundered in Cardigan Bay in 1974 while being used as a trial target. It lies on its port side in about 31-36 m, best done on slack water by experienced divers, with a largely intact hull.

sites.depthNote: Coflein 31 m; Divernet tour 35-45 m range, 36 m on the seabed

s1.quote: A destroyer lying on her port side in 33m … both stern and bow twin 4” gun turrets are accessible … must be dived on a look but do not interfer basis

s2.quote: designated as a protected place under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986

access.value: Protected place (Protection of Military Remains Act 1986); look but do not touch

highlights.text: Twin 4-inch gun turrets at bow and stern

summary.text: A Hunt-class destroyer lost off Lowestoft in 1941, lying on her port side in about 33 m. Both gun turrets can be reached, but as a protected military wreck she is for observation only.

s1.quote: The wreck remains upright in 37m … in visibility of less than 5m … With permission from the Ministry of Defence

s2.quote: sits in around 37m of water … the visibility wasn't good. We had around five metres

s3.quote: may not be dived upon without permission from the Ministry of Defence

access.value: Protected military wreck; MoD permission needed to dive

summary.text: The first British warship lost in the First World War, a cruiser mined in 1914, sits upright but split in two around 37 m down about 40 miles off Harwich. Visits need Ministry of Defence permission, and visibility has been around 5 m.

s1.quote: the 15m-deep site … I asked eight or ten times for an excavation license and was refused

s2.quote: there is almost zero visibility for the diving team … protected under law as nationally important archaeological sites

access.value: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); diving by licence only

hazards.text: Almost zero visibility, work by touch
Dive windows only when tidal current eases

summary.text: A protected 16th-century wreck mound with bronze guns off Dunwich, Suffolk, in about 15 m. Silty water gives almost no visibility and entry is possible only at slack tide, so work there is by licensed teams.

More fish life on the east side

summary.text: A sheltered cove in the Skomer marine reserve on the Pembrokeshire coast, entered from a stony beach. Depth runs from 10 to 30 m, deeper on the west side, with pink sea fans and good fish life but strong currents beyond the bay mouth.
